# Problem 1.1

This problem invites you to learn more about the "exact" vs "approximate"
confidence intervals in the case of the parameter of a binomial distribution.
Concretely, for any $n\in \{10, 30, 50, 100\}$, and any
$\theta\in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9\}$ generate $N=10^5$ data sets from the resulting
binomial distribution. For each data set, compute

- the exact binomial 0.90 confidence interval
- the approximate 0.90 confidence interval (using the Z formula in the slides)
- the approximate 0.90 confidence interval used by \texttt{prop.test} command
  with the option \texttt{correct=FALSE}

For each $n$ and $\theta$, compute and report relative number of times the $N$
intervals trap $\theta$. That is, for any $n\in \{10, 30, 50, 100\}$, and for
any $\theta\in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9\}$, generate $N=10^5$ binomial random numbers and
for of these compute the above intervals. For the $10^5$ intervals report the
fraction of times $\theta$ is in it.

Show your results by means of suitable table or diagram and the results.

## Solution to Problem 1.1

The full stand-alone script is `problem_1_1.R`. The three intervals are

- **exact (Clopper–Pearson)**, obtained with `binom.test`, built by inverting
  the binomial tail probabilities;
- **Wald (Z)**, from the slides: $\hat\theta \pm z_{0.95}\sqrt{\hat\theta(1-\hat\theta)/n}$,
  with $\hat\theta = S/n$ and $z_{0.95}\approx 1.645$;
- **Wilson score**, obtained with `prop.test(..., correct = FALSE)`, i.e. the set
  of $\theta$ such that $|S/n-\theta|/\sqrt{\theta(1-\theta)/n} \le z_{0.95}$.

Since $S$ can only take the values $0,1,\dots,n$, each interval is computed once
for every possible outcome $s$ and then looked up for the $N$ simulated counts.
This gives exactly the same result as calling `binom.test`/`prop.test` on each of
the $10^5$ data sets, at a tiny fraction of the cost.

```{r p11-sim}
set.seed(47)
ns     <- c(10, 30, 50, 100)
thetas <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
N      <- 1e5
level  <- 0.90
z      <- qnorm(1 - (1 - level) / 2)   # 1.645

# ---- intervals for every possible outcome s = 0, ..., n --------------------
# each function returns a (n + 1) x 2 matrix: [lower, upper]

ci_exact <- function(n, level) {
  t(sapply(0:n, function(s) binom.test(s, n, conf.level = level)$conf.int))
}

ci_wald <- function(n, level) {
  z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - level) / 2)
  p <- (0:n) / n
  cbind(p - z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n), p + z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n))
}

ci_score <- function(n, level) {
  t(sapply(0:n, function(s)
    prop.test(s, n, conf.level = level, correct = FALSE)$conf.int))
}

methods <- list(
  "Exact (Clopper-Pearson)"      = ci_exact,
  "Wald (Z)"                     = ci_wald,
  "Score (prop.test, no corr.)"  = ci_score
)

# ---- simulation ------------------------------------------------------------
res <- expand.grid(n = ns, theta = thetas, method = names(methods),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res$coverage <- NA_real_

for (n in ns) {
  # intervals for all possible outcomes, for every method
  cis <- lapply(methods, function(f) f(n, level))
  for (theta in thetas) {
    S <- rbinom(N, size = n, prob = theta)   # N simulated data sets
    for (m in names(methods)) {
      lo <- cis[[m]][S + 1, 1]
      up <- cis[[m]][S + 1, 2]
      res$coverage[res$n == n & res$theta == theta & res$method == m] <-
        mean(lo <= theta & theta <= up)
    }
  }
}

# ---- table -----------------------------------------------------------------
tab <- reshape(res, idvar = c("theta", "n"), timevar = "method",
               direction = "wide")
names(tab) <- sub("coverage.", "", names(tab), fixed = TRUE)
tab <- tab[order(tab$theta, tab$n), ]
rownames(tab) <- NULL
```

```{r p11-table}
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 4,
             caption = "Empirical coverage of the nominal 0.90 intervals")
```

```{r p11-plot, fig.cap="Empirical coverage of the three 0.90 intervals (dotted line: nominal level)."}
cols <- c("black", "red", "blue")
pchs <- c(15, 16, 17)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (theta in thetas) {
  plot(NA, xlim = range(ns), ylim = c(0.6, 1), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "n", ylab = "Empirical coverage",
       main = bquote(theta == .(theta)))
  axis(1, at = ns)
  abline(h = level, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
  for (k in seq_along(methods)) {
    d <- res[res$theta == theta & res$method == names(methods)[k], ]
    lines(d$n, d$coverage, type = "b", col = cols[k], pch = pchs[k], lwd = 2)
  }
}
plot.new()   # 4th panel: legend
legend("center", legend = names(methods), col = cols, pch = pchs, lwd = 2,
       bty = "n", title = "Method")
```

**Comments.**

- **Exact (Clopper–Pearson).** Its coverage is *always* at least the nominal
  0.90, as guaranteed by construction, but it is conservative: for $n=10$ it
  traps $\theta$ about 98–99% of the times, and it is still around 0.93–0.94
  for $n=100$ when $\theta=0.1, 0.9$. The price is wider intervals than needed.
- **Wald (Z).** It is the worst method. For $\theta=0.5$ it behaves reasonably
  well (coverage 0.88–0.91), but for $\theta$ close to the boundaries the
  coverage is dramatically below the nominal level: $\approx 0.64$ for $n=10$,
  $\approx 0.79$ for $n=30$ and still only $\approx 0.86$ for $n=100$. The
  reason is that the normal approximation of $\hat\theta$ is poor when
  $n\theta$ or $n(1-\theta)$ is small, and the estimated standard error
  $\sqrt{\hat\theta(1-\hat\theta)/n}$ is very unreliable (when $S=0$ or $S=n$
  the interval degenerates to a single point).
- **Score (`prop.test`, `correct = FALSE`).** It is the best compromise: its
  coverage oscillates *around* the nominal value (0.87–0.93) for all $n$ and
  $\theta$, without the systematic under-coverage of Wald and without the
  over-coverage of the exact interval.
- For $\theta=0.5$ the Wald and the score intervals give exactly the same
  coverage: the intervals differ, but they contain $\theta=0.5$ for the same
  values of $s$.
- Results for $\theta=0.1$ and $\theta=0.9$ are (up to simulation error)
  identical, by symmetry ($S \mapsto n-S$).
- Coverage is not a monotone function of $n$: because $S$ is discrete, the set of
  outcomes $s$ whose interval contains $\theta$ changes in jumps, producing the
  well known "oscillating" behaviour of binomial coverage probabilities.

# Problem 1.2

This problem invites you to learn more about the continuity correction in the
context of confidence intervals for the the parameter of a binomial
distribution. In particular,

- read Newcombe (1998) article;
- repeat the experiments in Problem 1, now applying the continuity correction to
  all possible methods.

Show your results by means of suitable diagram and compare the results with the
previous ones. Conclusions?

## Solution to Problem 1.2

The full stand-alone script is `problem_1_2.R`. Following Newcombe (1998), the
methods with and without continuity correction (CC) are:

| Method | without CC | with CC |
|:-------|:-----------|:--------|
| Wald | $\hat\theta \pm z\sqrt{\hat\theta(1-\hat\theta)/n}$ (method 1) | $\hat\theta \pm \left(z\sqrt{\hat\theta(1-\hat\theta)/n} + \frac{1}{2n}\right)$ (method 2) |
| Score (Wilson) | `prop.test(correct = FALSE)` (method 3) | `prop.test(correct = TRUE)` (method 4) |
| Exact | mid-$p$ interval (method 6) | Clopper–Pearson, `binom.test` (method 5) |

For the exact family the Clopper–Pearson interval already plays the role of the
"continuity corrected" interval: its limits solve
$P_\theta(S\ge s)=\alpha/2$ and $P_\theta(S\le s)=\alpha/2$, i.e. they count the
*whole* probability of the observed value $s$ in the tails. The uncorrected
counterpart is the mid-$p$ interval, whose limits solve
$P_\theta(S>s)+\tfrac12 P_\theta(S=s)=\alpha/2$ and
$P_\theta(S<s)+\tfrac12 P_\theta(S=s)=\alpha/2$. The Wald + CC limits are
truncated to $[0,1]$.

The same seed as in Problem 1.1 is used, so all methods are evaluated on
exactly the same simulated data sets. Besides the coverage we also record the
mean width of the intervals, to quantify the cost of the correction.

```{r p12-sim}
set.seed(47)
ns     <- c(10, 30, 50, 100)
thetas <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
N      <- 1e5
level  <- 0.90
alpha  <- 1 - level

# ---- intervals for every possible outcome s = 0, ..., n --------------------

ci_wald <- function(n, level, cc = FALSE) {
  z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - level) / 2)
  p <- (0:n) / n
  half <- z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n) + cc / (2 * n)
  cbind(pmax(0, p - half), pmin(1, p + half))   # truncated to [0, 1]
}

ci_score <- function(n, level, cc = FALSE) {
  t(sapply(0:n, function(s)
    prop.test(s, n, conf.level = level, correct = cc)$conf.int))
}

ci_exact <- function(n, level) {               # Clopper-Pearson
  t(sapply(0:n, function(s) binom.test(s, n, conf.level = level)$conf.int))
}

ci_midp <- function(n, level) {                # mid-p exact interval
  a <- (1 - level) / 2
  t(sapply(0:n, function(s) {
    # lower: P(S > s) + P(S = s)/2 = a ; upper: P(S < s) + P(S = s)/2 = a
    lo <- if (s == 0) 0 else uniroot(function(th)
      pbinom(s, n, th, lower.tail = FALSE) + 0.5 * dbinom(s, n, th) - a,
      c(0, 1), tol = 1e-10)$root
    up <- if (s == n) 1 else uniroot(function(th)
      pbinom(s - 1, n, th) + 0.5 * dbinom(s, n, th) - a,
      c(0, 1), tol = 1e-10)$root
    c(lo, up)
  }))
}

methods <- list(
  "Wald"            = function(n, l) ci_wald(n, l, cc = FALSE),
  "Wald + CC"       = function(n, l) ci_wald(n, l, cc = TRUE),
  "Score"           = function(n, l) ci_score(n, l, cc = FALSE),
  "Score + CC"      = function(n, l) ci_score(n, l, cc = TRUE),
  "Exact mid-p"     = ci_midp,
  "Exact C-P (CC)"  = ci_exact
)

# ---- simulation (same random numbers as in Problem 1.1) -------------------
res <- expand.grid(n = ns, theta = thetas, method = names(methods),
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res$coverage <- NA_real_
res$width    <- NA_real_

for (n in ns) {
  cis <- lapply(methods, function(f) f(n, level))
  for (theta in thetas) {
    S <- rbinom(N, size = n, prob = theta)
    for (m in names(methods)) {
      lo <- cis[[m]][S + 1, 1]
      up <- cis[[m]][S + 1, 2]
      idx <- res$n == n & res$theta == theta & res$method == m
      res$coverage[idx] <- mean(lo <= theta & theta <= up)
      res$width[idx]    <- mean(up - lo)
    }
  }
}

# ---- tables ----------------------------------------------------------------
wide <- function(var) {
  d <- reshape(res[, c("n", "theta", "method", var)],
               idvar = c("theta", "n"), timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
  names(d) <- sub(paste0(var, "."), "", names(d), fixed = TRUE)
  d <- d[order(d$theta, d$n), ]
  rownames(d) <- NULL
  d
}
tab_cov   <- wide("coverage")
tab_width <- wide("width")
```

```{r p12-tables}
knitr::kable(tab_cov, digits = 4,
             caption = "Empirical coverage, with and without continuity correction")
knitr::kable(tab_width, digits = 3,
             caption = "Mean width of the intervals")
```

```{r p12-plots, fig.cap=c("Empirical coverage (solid: no CC, dashed: with CC; dotted line: nominal level).", "Mean width of the intervals (solid: no CC, dashed: with CC).")}
cols <- c("red", "red", "blue", "blue", "darkgreen", "darkgreen")
ltys <- c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2)
pchs <- c(16, 1, 17, 2, 15, 0)

plot_res <- function(var, ylim, ylab, hline = NULL) {
  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
  for (theta in thetas) {
    plot(NA, xlim = range(ns), ylim = ylim, xaxt = "n",
         xlab = "n", ylab = ylab, main = bquote(theta == .(theta)))
    axis(1, at = ns)
    if (!is.null(hline)) abline(h = hline, lty = 3, col = "gray40")
    for (k in seq_along(methods)) {
      d <- res[res$theta == theta & res$method == names(methods)[k], ]
      lines(d$n, d[[var]], type = "b", col = cols[k], lty = ltys[k],
            pch = pchs[k], lwd = 2)
    }
  }
  plot.new()   # 4th panel: legend
  legend("center", legend = names(methods), col = cols, lty = ltys,
         pch = pchs, lwd = 2, bty = "n", title = "Method")
}

plot_res("coverage", ylim = c(0.6, 1), ylab = "Empirical coverage",
         hline = level)
plot_res("width", ylim = c(0, max(res$width)), ylab = "Mean interval width")
```

**Comparison with Problem 1.1 and conclusions.**

- The "Wald", "Score" and "Exact C-P" columns coincide with the results of
  Problem 1.1 (same data sets): the new information is given by the corrected
  Wald and score intervals and by the mid-$p$ interval.
- **The continuity correction always widens the interval** (it moves both
  limits outwards), and therefore the coverage can only increase. On the
  other hand the mean width increases too: e.g. for $n=10$, $\theta=0.5$ the
  score interval goes from $\approx 0.44$ to $\approx 0.50$; the relative cost
  becomes small as $n$ grows ($\approx 0.16$ vs $0.17$ for $n=100$).
- **Wald + CC** improves the Wald interval for $n\ge 30$, but it does not cure
  its fundamental defect: for $n=10$, $\theta=0.1$ (or $0.9$) the coverage is
  still $\approx 0.65$, since when $S=0$ the interval is just
  $[0, 1/(2n)] = [0, 0.05]$, which cannot contain $\theta = 0.1$; its coverage
  is moreover very erratic (0.95 for $n=30$, 0.88 for $n=50$). Wald-type
  intervals remain unreliable with or without correction.
- **Score + CC** (`prop.test` default) is conservative: its coverage is never
  below 0.90 and behaves very much like the Clopper–Pearson interval (in many
  cells the coverage is even identical), sometimes being even more
  conservative (e.g. 0.974 vs 0.931 for $n=30$, $\theta=0.1$).
- **Mid-$p$** (the "uncorrected exact" interval) behaves like the uncorrected
  score interval: coverage close to 0.90 on average, sometimes slightly below
  (minimum $\approx 0.88$), with narrower intervals than Clopper–Pearson.
- Hence the methods split in two groups, as pointed out by Newcombe (1998):
    - *uncorrected* methods (score, mid-$p$) aim at a **mean** coverage
      close to $1-\alpha$, accepting that for some $(n,\theta)$ the coverage
      is slightly lower;
    - *corrected* methods (score + CC, Clopper–Pearson) aim at a **minimum**
      coverage of $1-\alpha$, at the price of being conservative (wider
      intervals, coverage often well above $1-\alpha$).
- Conclusion: the Wald interval (with or without CC) should be avoided,
  especially for small $n$ or $\theta$ close to 0 or 1. If we want an
  interval whose coverage is on average close to the nominal level, the score
  interval without CC (or the mid-$p$ interval) is the best choice; if we
  require the coverage to be *never* below the nominal level, the
  continuity-corrected score interval or the exact Clopper–Pearson interval
  should be used. This agrees with Newcombe's recommendation of the score
  method (with or without CC) and of the exact/mid-$p$ methods.

# Problem 1.3

According de Moivre-Laplace's theorem, $W$ must converge to the standard normal
distribution as $n$ increases. You are invited to illustrate one aspect of this
fact via simulations as follows. For each $\theta \in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9\}$ and for
each $n \in\{30,50,100,150, 300, 500\}$, generate $N=10^5$ random numbers of $W$
and approximate $p_{n,\theta} = P(-0.5\leq W_\theta\leq -0.1)$ by $\hat p_n$,
given by the relative frequency of $W_\theta$'s that satisfy the inequality.
Plot the pairs $(n ,\hat{p}_{n,\theta})$ for all $n$, for each $\theta$ along
with the target value provided by the aforementioned theorem. Comment the
results.

## Solution to Problem 1.3

The full stand-alone script is `problem_1_3.R`. With $S\sim \text{Bin}(n,\theta)$,
$$
W_\theta = \frac{S-n\theta}{\sqrt{n\theta(1-\theta)}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1),
$$
so the target value is
$p_\infty = \Phi(-0.1)-\Phi(-0.5) \approx `r round(pnorm(-0.1) - pnorm(-0.5), 4)`$.
For reference, the exact value of $p_{n,\theta}$, computed from the binomial
distribution, is also reported.

```{r p13-sim}
set.seed(47)
ns     <- c(30, 50, 100, 150, 300, 500)
thetas <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
N      <- 1e5
a <- -0.5
b <- -0.1

target <- pnorm(b) - pnorm(a)    # limit value given by the theorem

res <- expand.grid(n = ns, theta = thetas)
res$p_hat   <- NA_real_
res$p_exact <- NA_real_

for (i in seq_len(nrow(res))) {
  n     <- res$n[i]
  theta <- res$theta[i]
  sd    <- sqrt(n * theta * (1 - theta))
  S <- rbinom(N, size = n, prob = theta)
  W <- (S - n * theta) / sd
  res$p_hat[i] <- mean(a <= W & W <= b)
  # exact: P(n theta + a sd <= S <= n theta + b sd)
  s_vals <- 0:n
  w_vals <- (s_vals - n * theta) / sd
  res$p_exact[i] <- sum(dbinom(s_vals[a <= w_vals & w_vals <= b], n, theta))
}
```

```{r p13-table}
knitr::kable(res, digits = 4,
             caption = "Simulated and exact values of P(-0.5 <= W <= -0.1)")
```

```{r p13-plot, fig.cap="Simulated relative frequencies (blue), exact binomial probabilities (red crosses) and normal limit (dashed line)."}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
ylim <- range(c(0, res$p_hat, res$p_exact, target))
for (theta in thetas) {
  d <- res[res$theta == theta, ]
  plot(d$n, d$p_hat, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "blue",
       ylim = ylim, xlab = "n", ylab = expression(hat(p)[list(n, theta)]),
       main = bquote(theta == .(theta)), log = "x", xaxt = "n")
  axis(1, at = ns)
  points(d$n, d$p_exact, pch = 4, col = "red", cex = 1.5, lwd = 2)
  abline(h = target, lty = 2, lwd = 2)
}
plot.new()   # 4th panel: legend
legend("center", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Simulated (relative frequency)", "Exact binomial",
                  "Normal limit"),
       col = c("blue", "red", "black"), pch = c(16, 4, NA),
       lty = c(1, NA, 2), lwd = 2)
```

**Comments.**

- The simulated relative frequencies $\hat p_{n,\theta}$ practically coincide
  with the exact binomial probabilities $p_{n,\theta}$: with $N=10^5$ the Monte
  Carlo standard error is about $\sqrt{0.15\cdot 0.85/10^5}\approx 0.001$.
  Hence the discrepancies from the dashed line are **not** due to the
  simulation, but to the fact that, for finite $n$, $W_\theta$ is not normal.
- The convergence towards $p_\infty\approx 0.152$ is clearly **not
  monotone**: $\hat p_{n,\theta}$ oscillates around the target. The reason is
  that $W_\theta$ is a discrete random variable living on a lattice with step
  $1/\sqrt{n\theta(1-\theta)}$; the interval $[-0.5,-0.1]$, of length 0.4,
  contains either $\lfloor 0.4\sqrt{n\theta(1-\theta)}\rfloor$ or one more
  lattice point, depending on $n$, and each point carries a probability
  $\approx \varphi(w)/\sqrt{n\theta(1-\theta)}$. Including/excluding one point
  makes $\hat p$ jump above or below the target.
- The extreme case is $n=30$, $\theta=0.1$ (and $0.9$): here
  $\sqrt{n\theta(1-\theta)}\approx 1.64$ and
  $-0.5\le W\le -0.1 \iff 2.18\le S\le 2.84$, an interval containing no
  integer, so $p_{30,\theta}=0$ exactly, far from $0.152$.
- As $n$ grows the lattice becomes finer, each point carries less probability
  and the oscillations shrink (their amplitude is of order $1/\sqrt{n}$), so
  $\hat p_{n,\theta}\to p_\infty$, as stated by the de Moivre–Laplace theorem.
- The convergence is faster for $\theta=0.5$ than for $\theta=0.1$ or $0.9$:
  the effective sample size governing the approximation is $n\theta(1-\theta)$,
  which is maximal at $\theta=0.5$, and for $\theta \ne 0.5$ the binomial
  distribution is skewed, which further slows the convergence. Note also that
  the results for $\theta=0.1$ and $\theta=0.9$ are similar but not identical:
  the interval $[-0.5,-0.1]$ is not symmetric around 0, so it sees the two
  opposite skewnesses differently.
